title: IIT Roorkee Backtracks on Advisory Warning Students Against Political Movements
excerpt: After social media backlash, the premier engineering institute clarified that an internal email asking students not to 'show affinity to political movements' was an annual advisory, not a new directive issued amid the ongoing CJP protests.
body:
• IIT Roorkee sent an advisory to students warning them not to "show affinity to political movements like the one currently," a reference to the ongoing Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protests against the NEET paper leak.
  • The advisory cited the institute's conduct rules, which prohibit statements "capable of embarrassing the relations between the Institute and the Central Government."
  • After widespread criticism on social media, IIT Roorkee clarified the communication was an "internal advisory issued annually" and not a new directive.
  • The episode comes as CJP-led protests demanding the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan have drawn tens of thousands of demonstrators to Delhi's Jantar Mantar.

The Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee found itself scrambling to contain a social media firestorm after an internal advisory warned students and staff against showing political sympathies — a communication widely perceived as an attempt to discourage participation in the growing student-led protests sweeping India.

The advisory, portions of which were shared on social media platforms, instructed students not to "show affinity to political movements like the one currently" and cautioned against making statements or taking actions that could embarrass the institute's relationship with the central government. The language drew directly from IIT Roorkee's Appendix D conduct rules, which state that no member shall make any statement "capable of embarrassing the relations between the Institute and the Central Government or any State Government."

Backlash and Backtrack

The timing of the advisory proved explosive. It surfaced just as tens of thousands of protesters gathered at Delhi's Jantar Mantar on July 20 for the Cockroach Janta Party's "Chalo Sansad" march, demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak. Critics immediately interpreted the advisory as an institutional attempt to silence students sympathetic to the movement.

Facing intense scrutiny online, IIT Roorkee issued a clarification on July 21, stating that the communication was "an internal advisory issued annually to students and staff" and not a new directive. The institute said the advisory had been "misinterpreted as a ban on supporting student protests online."

"This communication is an internal advisory issued annually to students and staff."

— IIT Roorkee, in its clarification statement

A Pattern at India's Elite Institutions

The controversy at IIT Roorkee is not an isolated incident. India's premier engineering and management institutes have a fraught history with student political expression. During the 2019 protests against the Citizenship Amendment Act, IIT Kanpur launched an inquiry against students who recited a protest poem, and the Ministry of Human Resource Development was forced to deny reports that IITs had been instructed to monitor students' social media posts.

Earlier this year, IIT Roorkee itself made headlines for canceling a memorandum of understanding with a Turkish university on national interest grounds, and the institute has previously warned against "misleading content" being shared on social media that could tarnish its reputation.

The conduct rules cited in the advisory — which apply to employees and have been extended to students — date back to the institution's older governance frameworks. Legal experts have questioned whether such blanket restrictions on political expression can be applied to students at public-funded universities, which are expected to serve as spaces for open debate and intellectual inquiry.

The Broader Student Protest Movement

The advisory emerged against a backdrop of India's most significant student protest in recent years. The CJP movement, which began in May 2026 as an online satirical response to Chief Justice of India Surya Kant's remarks comparing unemployed youth to "cockroaches," has transformed into a mass political movement. It now claims over 22 million Instagram followers and has organized sustained protests at Jantar Mantar since June 6.

Activist Sonam Wangchuk's indefinite hunger strike beginning June 28 galvanized the movement further. On July 18, police forcibly removed Wangchuk from the protest site and admitted him to Safdarjung Hospital. Two days later, the "Chalo Sansad" march saw police use tear gas and lathi charges against demonstrators, leaving at least 118 police personnel and approximately 60 protesters injured, according to hospital authorities.

The movement's core demand — the resignation of Education Minister Pradhan over the NEET paper leak — has drawn support from opposition parties, prominent civil society figures, and student organizations including the All India Students Association and Students Federation of India.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indian-origin families abroad, many of whom view IIT admission as a prestigious milestone, the episode raises uncomfortable questions about academic freedom at India's elite institutions. IIT alumni, a significant presence in Silicon Valley, Wall Street, and global academia, have historically championed their alma maters as bastions of meritocracy and intellectual rigor. An institution appearing to restrict political expression — even if described as routine — complicates that narrative at a time when the broader education system faces a credibility crisis over exam leaks.

Looking Ahead

The CJP-led protests show no sign of abating. Protesters have already reclaimed the Jantar Mantar site after police dismantled their stage overnight. CJP representatives met Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda on July 20 to present demands including Wangchuk's release, Pradhan's resignation, and ₹1 crore compensation for families of NEET aspirants who died by suicide. Nadda described the meeting as "fine" but made no commitments.

With Parliament's monsoon session underway, opposition parties have vowed to raise the NEET controversy and police action on the floor. Whether IIT Roorkee's hastily retracted advisory becomes a footnote or a flashpoint in the broader debate over academic freedom in India remains to be seen.
